Cassini didn't just run out of fuel. Keeping it in a stable orbit meant the chances of it drifting into Enceladus or Titan were non-zero, and a dead or tumbling probe would be far more dangerous than a targeted crash. The plan was to plunge it into Saturn's upper atmosphere on purpose, which also let it take readings right up to the end.

The idea of crashing into the planet wasn't just cleanup. It was a way to keep those moons clean for the science that comes after, while still squeezing one last set of measurements out of the mission. The endgame worked out better than most people expect for a spacecraft's final act.

Your stationary leg is taking a beating, and it's not because the board is bad. Skateboarding is a lopsided workout. The pushing leg does the obvious work, but the other leg is still doing a ton you can't see. It has to stay locked and balanced while the body moves side to side and up and down over every bump, curb and rail. That constant tension builds up heat and lactic acid faster than people expect.

Then there's the stance thing. If you're regular or goofy, one foot is always in front. That front foot is the one staying put while you push off with the other. It's like doing hundreds of small isometric holds with a weight on top of your foot. The calf, the ankle joint, and the ligaments around it are doing more than you realize. You're not pushing with it, but you're not letting it rest either.

A lot of people get confused because the pain can show up in the knee or even the hip, not the ankle. That's because the whole chain above the foot takes the shock. Your tibia and knee cap take the impact, so if the pain is in the front of the shin, it's the same problem showing up lower down.

Try a simple test. If the pain is mostly on one specific leg, that's your pushing leg, and it's from overuse and from the impact of landing. If it's the other one, it's the stationary leg doing its quiet work. Either way, it's not a board problem and not your form being wrong.

The fix is less about "rest" and more about balance. Do a few weeks of alternating the push leg, or just ride slower and land softer. Add some simple ankle and calf stretches, maybe a few minutes of balance work on the board. If the pain gets sharp or starts locking the joint, see a physio, but for the usual aching, it's just overworked tissue asking for a break.

The name "Afro-American" (or African-American) sticks to that African root, even if most people don't have recent family ties to the continent. That root is the point, not a claim that everyone is from a specific country. The term shows up because the ancestry matters in history, and people still use both "African American" and "Black American" casually.

In practice, most use "Black American" day to day, and the Afro- label is just a formal variant that points back to that origin. I wouldn't expect everyone to name a country when asked, the label works as a broad grouping, not a passport.

Mostly the borders are the answer. The lines next to Turkey, Iraq, Jordan and Lebanon leak in guns and ammo with astonishing ease, and smugglers have routes that make checkpoints look decorative. State-issued stuff gets diverted too, and during the civil war weapons simply stopped being precious.

They still get them because there's no shortage of demand. A militia needs fresh supplies just to hold ground, and the market has learned to work around checkpoints and borders. It's a bit like buying everyday goods, except the goods are rifles and bullets.

That's a fair frustration, because "all drugs are bad" is a stretch. Plenty of drugs are genuinely useful for the right person. The question that actually needs answering is why the ones that make you feel great are usually also the ones that ruin you over time.

The short version is that the same system that throws you into euphoria is also where tolerance, dependency and the nasty side effects live. The brain doesn't care about your to-do list; it just wants things to return to its preferred state. A drug that hijacks reward strongly makes the brain adjust, and that adjustment is what turns a good feeling into a compulsion. The pleasure and the problems aren't separate things you can decouple with a smarter molecule; they're entangled in the same pathways. That's why something that feels incredible in the first hour can still be a nightmare in the first year.

I think a lot of the confusion is that we imagine a drug like a filter you can turn on and off. But most psychoactive substances act through receptors that also control breathing, heart rate, temperature, blood pressure and so on. You can't push the reward button without nudging the rest of the system. Some drugs are safer than others, and some are used in medicine because the benefits outweigh the costs, but "zero adverse effects" is a very high bar and most candidates that get close still show problems at higher doses or with repeated use.

There's also a practical wrinkle: the more a drug changes how your brain rewards itself, the more your body starts expecting it. That's tolerance. Withdrawal is the other side of the same coin. A drug that never does either is already exceptional, and most candidates fall short in one of those two ways.

So no, not all drugs are bad. But yes, the intense-euphoria ones tend to come with a bill you pay later, and the chemistry of getting the good feeling and the chemistry of the downsides are usually in the same room.

Hi [friend],

The pain's real, and it makes sense once you see what's actually happening. It's not a headache, it's the constant low-grade strain of matching her pace. You're on your feet most of the day, and your lower back is doing quiet, heavy work to stay upright while you walk. Add the hot, stuffy aisles and the noise, and that background effort is enough to make your head ache in a way that's different from a normal headache. It's not a mystery, it's just your body flagging the sustained effort.

Take a sit every hour or so and you'll feel it ease.

Best,
Sam

Hi,

It's a tongue twister. Saying "silk" five times primes your mouth for rhyming words, and "milk" is right there as the closest match. So when he asked what cows drink, your mouth just went to the word it was already shaped to say. It's not that you didn't know cows drink water.

You're not wrong about cows. They do drink water, obviously. The "milk" answer was just your tongue finishing the rhyme instead of your brain answering the question.

That's the fun and the frustration of them, I guess. Next time he does this, just say water out loud. You already knew the right answer, your mouth just took the easy rhyme.

Best,
Sam

Hi,

Thanks for reaching out, and yes, I'm happy to talk through it. For a first home, start with what you can actually afford, not just what the bank will lend. Factor in the mortgage, council tax, insurance, and a realistic buffer for repairs. A common mistake is focusing only on the monthly payment and forgetting that an old house can have expensive surprises, so get a proper survey and check the service connections before you get attached to a property.

I'd also think about where you'll need to live long term. A cheaper house in a great area is often better than a bigger one in a place you won't want to stay in. Check schools, commute times, and what's within walking distance. The neighborhood matters more than the number of bedrooms.

For the questions themselves, send them over and I'll go through each one properly. If they're about surveys, mortgages, or legal steps, I can point you to the right places and flag anything that tends to trip people up.

Let's keep it to a few focused questions rather than a general chat, so I can give you answers you can actually use.

Best,
Alex

Hi,

A 3-in-1 isn't a mix of three separate products. It's mostly one big surfactant system doing the whole job, which is why it works on skin and hair at the same time. The 2-in-1 already uses that same blending logic; the 3-in-1 just widens it to cover bodywash territory too.

What you'd miss by switching to separate products is a bit of convenience, but you'd get back some control. Shampoo has its own balance of cleanser and conditioning agents, conditioner is basically mostly emollients, and a bodywash is tuned for skin, not hair. A combo has to keep all of that in one bottle, so it tends to be gentler and milder than any of the dedicated versions.

For me the trade-off is fine for quick days, but if your hair is doing something odd, I'd go back to the separate stuff for a while.

Thanks for the question,
Sam

They use GPS. Survey teams place receivers on bedrock and keep recording for years, then compare the positions to satellites orbiting overhead. The tiny shifts in latitude and longitude give you the drift, and because the satellites move fast and the ground is moving too, they can model how plates are sliding past each other, which lets them get the continent's speed.

The scale is the fun part. North America is creeping west and south about four centimeters a year, while the Pacific plate slides under it, which is what keeps the ring of volcanoes and earthquakes you're used to seeing along the coast. For the continent's net motion, you're looking at roughly a meter every few years, which is a lot for something so huge, but it takes decades to feel.

If you want a single number to start from, think in centimeters a year, and I can point you to a live page of GPS data if you want to see the raw numbers behind the plate models.

Sam

Inbreeding lowers average IQ mainly because related parents share a lot of the same genes, which means they're more likely to pass on matching recessive alleles. In a normal family, rare bad copies of genes are usually hidden behind a healthy one from the other parent. When parents are closely related, the chance that both carry the same recessive mutation goes up, so it gets expressed more often.

The effects pile up. There are thousands of small-effect genes that influence brain development and learning, and each one adds a little drag on cognitive outcomes. When relatives mate, that hidden load shows through in the children more often, so the average IQ tends to fall below the population mean. It's not that one specific "IQ gene" breaks; it's many small effects adding together.

That's why the gap appears as a statistical average, not a guarantee about any single child.

The arm isn't special, it just gives you more options for managing the pain. You can rest it, brace it with a towel and a magazine, and keep it elevated without lying flat. That combination changes how you experience the injury.

I'd put an injured arm up on a pillow while lying down, and the swelling eases a lot. The pressure and position matter more than the type of cut or bruise itself.

A shoulder or upper arm injury also has the benefit that you can protect it more easily than, say, a rib. You don't have to twist or bear weight through it, which reduces the ongoing irritation.

It's not that the arm is tougher, it's that you can control what happens to it. That control is a big part of why it feels more manageable.

Carbon monoxide is nasty to breathe because it binds to hemoglobin in your blood far more tightly than oxygen does. When CO hangs onto your red blood cells, it squeezes the oxygen off and takes its place. Your blood stops carrying the oxygen your organs need, so your tissues start suffocating even though you are still breathing air. The body can barely notice it, which is what makes CO so dangerous. The classic symptom is a dull headache and dizziness that people often mistake for being a bit unwell or running a low fever, so you might ignore it until it gets bad.

Carbon dioxide is different because it does not lock onto your hemoglobin the way CO does. At the low levels people usually encounter, your lungs handle CO2 efficiently. You can feel it when levels rise enough to make you tired or give you a pounding headache, but your blood still moves oxygen properly. CO2 is a waste gas your body is built to exhale, and that is why it is not as poisonous.

The real difference comes down to binding strength. CO grabs hemoglobin with about 200 times the affinity of oxygen, while CO2 simply dissolves and gets pumped out through the lungs. CO sticks around until your lungs can push it off, which takes time even with fresh air. CO2 does not wait for you to notice.

One more thing worth knowing: the colorless, nearly odorless quality of CO is what makes it sneaky. Carbon dioxide does have a faint smell, and high CO2 produces a clear, unpleasant feeling, which gives you a warning. For a wiki, the key distinction is that CO blocks oxygen transport in the blood, whereas CO2 does not.

The brace position doesn't stop the impact, it redirects it. In a crash, the forward motion is the real danger, and the position keeps you from being thrown into seats or the floor. Hands on knees, head down, feet flat is the basic shape, and it spreads the load across your legs and spine rather than neck and arms taking all of it.

It's not about being rigid, and being too rigid can hurt your own neck. Most of the value is that your body moves as one piece with the seat, instead of you bouncing off it. If you've ever been in a bad bumpy ride where you weren't braced, you know the feeling of everything slamming forward. That's what this position reduces.

For a new colleague, the short version is: get low, protect your head and neck, let the seat do the work, and don't fight the impact with stiff muscles.

Most companies don't last. New ones start up and others fade out, so the oldest firms around are genuinely rare. A few are well known, and they did survive the industrial era. Their secret isn't that they're frozen in time, it's that they kept changing. They stopped being just what they started out as. So the honest answer is that there are some old businesses, and the ones that made it did so by reinventing themselves rather than staying the same.

I take the premise at face value: the dealership quote is the lower advertised rate, and I'll assume the dealer isn't hiding fees in the rate. That still leaves room for the bank to be cheaper, and the gap usually has to do with what the advertised number actually covers.

The dealer's headline rate typically comes with conditions you don't see until you're sitting at the desk. The low rate might only be for a short term, or only on certain models, and the fine print is what separates the sticker from the cost. A three-year promotional rate at the dealer might look amazing, but if you actually need five years of payments, you're paying the higher standard rate for the last two. The bank, with a longer standard term, can end up costing less over the life of the loan even with a higher starting rate.

There's also the question of what "cheaper" means. The dealer bundles things together, so the number on the page isn't the number you pay. You get the vehicle, the financing, the extended warranty, the paint protection and the tires all in one, and the financing portion is where the margin sits. The bank's job is only the loan, so what you're comparing is apples to a basket of fruit. If you take just the loan piece, the bank's cost is often less because there's no bundle to inflate it.

I've also seen that dealership rates are frequently conditional on a minimum term or a down payment, and the moment your situation doesn't fit the promo box, you land on the standard rate, which is usually the one you actually pay. The bank doesn't play that game as much. You get a quoted APR, you sign, that's the number.

A concrete comparison helps. Say the dealer offers 3% for three years on a $30,000 car with a $5,000 down payment. The bank offers 5% over five years. Over the dealer's three-year window, the dealer wins, but that's only if you can truly pay it off in three years. Most people can't. Once you stretch to five years, the dealer's promo expires and you pay standard rates, while the bank's flat five-year term stays at 5%. Total interest on the bank loan over five years is higher than the dealer's three-year interest, but per month and per dollar financed, the bank can still be the cheaper path for the person whose real cash flow is monthly, not quarterly.

The other part of it is fees. Banks charge less in origination fees and don't add dealer-installed accessories to the financed amount. That's a real difference, and it's one people often overlook because the APR is the number everyone argues about while the fees quietly eat the savings.

I'd say the advertised dealer rate is the easiest number to lose to, because it's the one they show you first, and the bank's cheaper path is the one you have to do the math on yourself.

I keep saying this and I'll keep getting told off for it, but I think most of the US has basically accepted marijuana, and the rest are catching up. If you're a US resident, you can probably smoke in 39 states. The law has gone quiet, which is the point.

The funny thing is the paperwork. You can walk into a legal dispensary, buy a pack of cigarettes, and nobody asks what you're doing. That ease is a statement. It's not that everyone's stoned; it's that no one's watching anymore.

I still think there's a gap in enforcement. The state legalizes, the federal law doesn't, and suddenly the same plant has two legal homes. That's the real problem people argue about, not the smoking itself.

People ask how the body makes electricity, and the short reality is that it’s not a battery or a power plant, it’s tiny voltage differences across cell membranes. Neurons stay polarized, sodium and potassium unevenly distributed. When a signal fires, sodium floods in and the potential flips briefly, then pumps restore the resting state. That’s it. No sparks, no lightning. My take: the body is an electrochemical machine, not a generator, and that distinction is what people keep missing.

Musicians sample older songs by cutting a small piece of audio and rebuilding it in a new song. You don't have to record the original again; you grab the existing sound and treat it like raw material. The tricky part is that the original artist or label usually owns that sound, so if the sample is recognizable and meaningful, you need permission. That permission process is where a lot of music gets delayed or killed.

The actual technique is less mysterious than people think. A producer takes a break, a horn line, a vocal phrase, or a whole drum pattern, loops it, changes the tempo or pitch, layers other sounds on top, and pushes it through effects. Sometimes the sample is obvious, sometimes it's chopped so small that you can't identify the source unless you're hunting for it. That hunting is half the fun for a lot of listeners.

My position is that sampling is one of the most creative uses of old music. It turns a song into a starting point instead of a finished thing. But it's not free. If you take a chunk from a classic track and it becomes central to your new song, the original rights holder can ask for a share of the money. That means clearing the sample can cost a lot or take a long time, which is why some songs stay stuck in production. A lot of producers have learned to cut a sample so short or alter it so heavily that it doesn't need clearing, though that's a judgment call, not a safe legal rule.

I like that sampling keeps old songs alive in a different form. A song from the 70s can become a beat for a new track, and both songs stay in circulation. The new song borrows a piece of the old song's soul, and the old song gains a second life.

The thing people miss is that sampling is as much about respect for the source as it is about getting something new to listen to. Done well, it connects generations of listeners without anyone having to go back and dig through crates. The music is still there, just wearing a different coat.

The question keeps coming up, so here’s my take. A headache isn’t just “my head hurts” with no cause. The blood vessels in the head swell and stretch, and the nerve endings that wrap around them get rubbed or pinched. That irritation is the actual source of the throbbing.

Stress, lack of sleep, dehydration, or certain foods can set the whole thing off. Your brain starts sending signals that the body reads as pain. There’s no mystery to it: it’s a real physical irritation, not a random nuisance.

It also helps to name the triggers in your own life. If your headaches always follow a bad night’s sleep or a big coffee withdrawal, that’s the pattern to work with. Fixing the usual cause is the best move, and the headache tends to fade once you address it.

I can’t even tell you if the food is good because we never got to eat. We got there at 7:20 p.m. on Sunday, specifically picking this place because our 10 p.m. show was in the same hotel, so I figured dining there would be easy. We put our names on the digital waitlist, which was completely useless, and were told to come back at 8:23 p.m. to pay. We did exactly that, then just stood around until 8:40 p.m. before staff casually said we probably wouldn’t be seated until 9:15 p.m. It was only a party of two, yet they offered zero solutions. If the wait stretches that far past payment, say so upfront instead of letting our night go completely to waste. Total disaster. I’d give it zero stars if that were an option.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and surprisingly, there was no line at all. Two people came out to about $130, which felt pretty steep. Before going, I figured the price would be comparable to a steakhouse. Afterward, I learned the buffet actually cost somewhat more than what I had expected to pay at one.

I was disappointed that steak wasn’t offered. At that price, I assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices included lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those are things you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn’t run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. The problem was that there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn’t want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station didn’t seem especially distinctive. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn’t try any.

I’d call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you’re curious, it’s worth trying once, especially if there’s no wait. But if the line is long, I’d probably reconsider.

The space bar rattles. Hit it with the edge of your thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key also repeats now and then, so "example" comes out as "eexample" and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I'm typing fast and not looking.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway, because of the switches. The seller took a week to answer what they were, so I'd already pulled off a keycap and found out for myself. They're brown tactile switches, a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle.

Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I'd have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now.

I've been to Vegas nearly my whole life, well, the under-21 version, so I've sat through a lot of shows before I could gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught, and it was mixed, maybe a bit worse than mixed.

The good part first: the circular stage is clever. You're looking down into it, so from almost any seat you get a decent view, which is rare in Vegas. Some individual acts are impressive, the strength stuff, the aerialists, the divers. Those people are athletes, no question. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil. Not exactly a rip-off, just, if you've seen Cirque, you've seen comparable feats with a bit more clarity. And clarity is the problem. What's the story? I still don't know. A dream? A guy? Water? It felt like a bunch of pretty images thrown at you, and the show never told me what it was trying to say. Also, there's way too much happening at once. Too many people, too many elements, too many "wow" moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. It felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle approach, where more must be better, so they crammed everything in.

Ticket note: if you're staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal, $99 instead of the usual $125. That helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn't pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn't blown away, and I don't think anyone else was either. That said, a few friends liked it, and if you've never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don't expect to leave overwhelmed.

Around two years ago, we ordered two shirts for my dad from Rockmount Ranch Wear by phone. The sales rep wrote down the delivery address wrong: her handwritten 7 got read as a 1. The address should've been 5407, but the package went to 5401. The people living at 5401 took it to the local UPS store to get it sent back, then it just vanished, and nobody ever heard from the company again. We found out several weeks later. While the dispute was going on, we placed another order for two shirts. Rockmount refused to refund the original two. At that point, the owner stepped in. He admitted the shipment went to the wrong address, but said no refund would happen unless the shirts were returned. He also blamed us for not being friendly enough to the residents of 5401, which is four doors away. We pushed back on the original charge with our credit card company and finally got a credit.
